name: Kogao massage

card.summary: A Japanese "small face" massage using hand strokes along the jaw, cheeks and neck, aimed at a slimmer-looking, more defined face.

quick.overview:
Kogao, Japanese for "small face", is both a beauty ideal and the name for facial massage routines aimed at a slimmer-looking face with a sharper jawline.

Proponents describe it as encouraging fluid movement and relaxing facial and neck muscles so the face looks less puffy and more defined.
quick.how: Practitioners use hands or fingers, often with oil or cream, in strokes along the jawline, cheeks and neck toward the lymph nodes. It is done at salons or at home, typically as a regular routine.
quick.risks: Gentle massage is generally low risk, though pressure on irritated or acne-prone skin may cause redness, and people with skin conditions or recent procedures are usually advised to check with a clinician.

lead: Kogao massage is a Japanese facial massage practice whose name means "small face". People use it to make the face look slimmer, less puffy and more contoured, particularly along the jaw and cheeks, with sessions often described as giving an immediate visual change.[1]

Practitioners describe light drainage-style strokes toward the neck and lymph nodes, followed in salons by firmer pressure on the facial muscles and jaw. Salon versions grew out of kogao kyosei ("small face correction"), described as developed in Japan by orthopaedic doctors with attention to muscle alignment, fascia release and lymphatic flow.[1]

The ideal behind it is older than the treatment: small-face ideals are prominent in Japanese beauty culture, and the cosmetics industry has long sold creams, masks and techniques toward them. Makeup trends from bronzer to contouring have pursued the same look.[3]

chain: Massage strokes along jaw, cheeks, neck
Temporary reduction of puffiness and muscle tension
Face looks slimmer and more defined
angle.text: Users do it to make the face appear slimmer and sharper, mostly through short-term de-puffing. Results are described as temporary and cumulative with regular use.

paras: The routine combines drainage-style strokes and muscle relaxation. Salon versions are done by therapists; home versions use hands, oil or tools.

A reported session lasted about 90 minutes: neck, back and head massage first, then facial massage and lymphatic drainage, with roughly 30 to 40 minutes of firmer "bone-shifting" pressure. Therapists assess the face and body first, since neck and shoulder tension is thought to affect sagging and asymmetry.[1]
Providers recommended weekly visits at first, then monthly maintenance, for the effect to hold.[1]

Small-face ideals are prominent in Japanese beauty culture. Over the following decades makeup styles changed repeatedly in pursuit of the same goal: bronze foundation in the late 1990s to bring features visually closer, enlarged-eye looks in the late 2000s, low straight brows in the early 2010s, and heavy blush with contouring around 2015.[3]

Practitioners say the work reduces puffiness and tension, and one salon-group executive quoted in coverage said poor technique is unlikely to cause harm but would likely give less visible results, while untrained practitioners making claims could be risky.[1] Dermatologists generally describe massage as able to reduce short-term swelling but not to change bone structure.

timeline.event: Blush and contouring styles aim at a compact-looking face.[3]
